notes: Section 68/69 arbitration challenge on charter misrepresentation inducement; Cooke J's analysis of arbitrator's reasoning is detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Torch Offshore arbitration challenge on deck-strength misrepresentation inducement
key_facts: Torch chartered the vessel Midnight Hunter from Cable Shipping on a Supplytime form for Gulf of Mexico pipe-laying work.
Owners had innocently misrepresented deck strength as 10 mt/sqm and that no under-deck pillars were needed for Torch's modular pipe-laying system.
The arbitrator rejected Torch's rescission claim for lack of inducement but awarded damages for breach of the deck-strength description.
Torch applied under sections 68 and 69 of the 1996 Act alleging failure to decide inducement by the second representation and wrong legal tests.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside or vary an arbitration award and for permission to appeal on questions of law arising from a time charter dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Both the section 68 and section 69 applications dismissed; section 70(2) barred the section 68 challenge because section 57 recourse had not been exhausted, and on the merits the arbitrator had addressed inducement and applied the correct test.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to exhaust section 57 recourse bars a section 68 challenge where clarification could have resolved ambiguity; where an arbitrator deals with linked misrepresentations in the context of the case as argued, there is no serious irregularity under section 68(2)(d); a finding of fact applying the real-and-substantive-part inducement test cannot be challenged under section 69.
legal_issues: Whether the arbitrator failed to deal with inducement by the second misrepresentation
Whether section 57 or section 70(2) barred the section 68 application
Whether the arbitrator applied the wrong test for inducement and loss of rescission by lapse of time
Whether permission to appeal should be granted under section 69

notes: Restricted-patient MHRT discharge challenge; Lord Hope's Reid treatability analysis and mandatory s73(1)(b) consideration are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: MHRT absolute discharge quashed for failure on conditional recall
key_facts: Mr Wilson, detained since 1963 after being found unfit to plead to murder, was treated as subject to a hospital and restriction order without limit of time.
The Mental Health Review Tribunal directed his absolute discharge but deferred it for 12 weeks so the Home Secretary could consider his wish to stand trial.
The Tribunal accepted it was not satisfied Mr Wilson suffered from psychopathic disorder but gave inadequate reasons and did not address section 73(1)(b).
The Secretary of State challenged the decision; the Tribunal consented to quashing but Mr Wilson opposed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Mental Health Review Tribunal decision directing absolute discharge of a restricted patient.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal decision quashed and the matter remitted to a fresh tribunal; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a tribunal is not satisfied under section 72(1)(b)(i) that a restricted patient has a qualifying mental disorder, it must still expressly consider under section 73(1)(b) whether it is appropriate for the patient to remain liable to recall; failure to do so vitiates the decision; treatability under Reid is wider than clinical treatability but did not affect the primary diagnosis conclusion here.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal erred in its approach to treatability under section 72
Whether section 73(1)(b) required consideration of conditional discharge when no disorder was found
Whether the Tribunal had power to defer absolute discharge
Whether inadequate reasons for rejecting medical evidence invalidated the decision

notes: IAT remittal JR on refugee family reunion and Article 8; fact-heavy but Collins J's reasoning on delay and family life is clear.

enrichment.short_title: JR of IAT remittal in refugee mother's entry clearance appeal
key_facts: An Ethiopian mother sought entry clearance to join her daughter, a refugee granted indefinite leave to remain in 1997 after arriving in 1990.
The entry clearance officer rejected the application on credibility and maintenance grounds; an adjudicator allowed the appeal under the refugee family reunion policy and Article 8.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal remitted the appeal, finding the adjudicator had not properly weighed the ECO's interview advantage and the long separation.
The claimant sought judicial review of the IAT's remittal decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision remitting an entry clearance appeal to a fresh adjudicator.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Collins J held the IAT was entitled to find the adjudicator erred in law; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A remittal is not a final determination and may be challenged by judicial review; where an adjudicator fails adequately to analyse whether a pre-asylum family unit and continuing family life existed under the refugee reunion policy and Article 8, and gives insufficient weight to credibility findings based on interviews, the IAT may lawfully set aside the decision; long delay weakens family reunion claims.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review lay against an IAT remittal order
Whether the IAT erred in overturning the adjudicator's Article 8 and family reunion findings
Whether the adjudicator properly assessed family life after many years' separation
Whether the claimant's age evidence and interview discrepancies were adequately considered

notes: Licensing Act 1964 s77 SHC appeal; Court of Appeal's late-night pub analysis follows clearly from Crown Court findings.

enrichment.short_title: Special hours certificate appeal on ancillary liquor at Lloyd's No 1
key_facts: Aaron Hitchcock sought a special hours certificate to extend licensing at Lloyd's No 1 Cafe-Bar in Norwich until midnight.
The Crown Court granted the SHC after finding the premises structurally adapted for music, dancing and substantial refreshment.
Stanley Burnton J quashed that decision on judicial review at Luminar Leisure's instance, holding the Crown Court had misdirected itself on ancillary sales.
The appeal concerned whether liquor sales during extra hours would truly be ancillary or merely a late-night pub extension.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against an Administrative Court decision quashing a Crown Court grant of a special hours certificate and remitting the appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Crown Court decision quashed; the court indicated a mandatory order requiring dismissal of the SHC appeal may be appropriate given the findings.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 77 of the 1964 Act, use and intended use refer to the licensee's purpose; the sale of intoxicating liquor must be ancillary to music, dancing and substantial refreshment for customers resorting to the premises during the extra permitted hours, not merely during other hours; a SHC must not license a late-night pub where the licensee's real purpose is extended drinking with token facilities.
legal_issues: Meaning of bona fide use and intended use in section 77(b)
Whether ancillary liquor sales are judged by all customers or only those using statutory facilities
Application of Richards v Bloxham and Carter v Bradbeer
Appropriate relief after quashing the Crown Court decision

notes: Consolidated Article 8 appeals distinguishing Shala; Kay LJ's analysis of CIPU bulletins and delay is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 appeals by Croatian Serbs: Shala delay argument rejected
key_facts: Janjanin and Musanovic, ethnic Serbs from Croatia, appealed IAT refusals of their claims to remain based on Article 8 private and family life.
Both had long undetermined asylum claims; Musanovic did valuable work for Head Start and Janjanin worked for the NHS; adjudicators had recommended exceptional leave.
They argued Home Office delay meant they would likely have obtained asylum or ELR earlier, making removal disproportionate after Shala.
Reliance on a CIPU bulletin using 'will' rather than 'may' for Croatian Serbs was abandoned when the Secretary of State produced the official wording.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals to the Court of Appeal against Immigration Appeal Tribunal decisions refusing Article 8 claims.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed; the court held the facts did not establish that prompt determination would likely have resulted in asylum or exceptional leave, distinguishing Shala.
enrichment.ratio: Delay in asylum processing may be relevant to Article 8 proportionality only where, but for the delay, the appellant would likely have been granted asylum or exceptional leave under a clear policy; without such likelihood, delay and valuable employment in the UK do not make removal disproportionate; Shala turned on its exceptional facts including Kosovo policy and established family life.
legal_issues: Application of Shala to delay in Croatian Serb asylum cases
Whether CIPU bulletins showed a likelihood of protection if claims were decided within six months
Whether Article 8 private life based on charity or NHS work outweighed immigration control
Whether the IAT erred in its proportionality balancing

notes: Jesus Fellowship housing benefit ECHR and ultra vires challenge; three-judge Court of Appeal analysis is comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Jesus Fellowship housing benefit refused for non-commercial tenancies
key_facts: Five Jesus Fellowship Church Style Three members claimed housing benefit for communal residences under agreements pooling income with the Church Trust.
The tribunal held their tenancy agreements were not on a commercial basis, so regulation 7(1)(a) treated them as not liable for rent and disentitled them to HB.
The 1998 amendment removed the requirement that the landlord reside with the tenant, widening exclusion for non-commercial arrangements.
Appellants argued ECHR discrimination and that the Social Security Advisory Committee was misled when the amendment was made.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Social Security Commissioner dismissing appeals against refusal of housing benefit.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all grounds; commerciality is a pure question of fact on which religious factors cannot be discounted; the SSAC was not misled about the amendment's scope.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 7(1)(a) requires a factual determination whether a tenancy is on a commercial basis; factors arising from religious communal living cannot be excluded from that assessment; Article 9 does not require the State to subsidise religious practice through housing benefit; non-contributory benefits are not Protocol 1 possessions under Carson; the 1998 amendment was not ultra vires because the SSAC was told communal religious groups might be caught.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal discriminated under Article 14 read with Articles 8, 9 or Protocol 1 Article 1
Whether religious manifestations must be excluded from the commerciality assessment
Whether housing benefit entitlement is a possession under Protocol 1 Article 1
Whether the 1998 regulation 7 amendment was ultra vires for misleading the SSAC

notes: Attorney General's Reference on misconduct in public office; comprehensive restatement of offence elements after R v G.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: ingredients of misconduct in public office after R v G
key_facts: CA died in police custody after being arrested following a nightclub assault; officers failed adequately to monitor his breathing over about 11 minutes.
Police officers were charged with manslaughter by gross negligence and misconduct in public office but acquitted on no-case submissions.
The judge directed acquittal on manslaughter for lack of causation and on misconduct for insufficient recklessness evidence.
The Attorney General referred questions on the ingredients of misconduct in public office and the required mental element.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1972 following directed acquittals at trial.
enrichment.outcome: Court answered the reference: misconduct requires wilful neglect or misconduct by a public officer to a degree amounting to abuse of public trust without reasonable excuse; recklessness follows the subjective test in R v G, not Caldwell; routine use of 'bad faith' in summing-up is disfavoured.
enrichment.ratio: Misconduct in public office at common law requires (1) a public officer acting as such, (2) wilful neglect or wilful misconduct, (3) conduct so far below standards as to amount to abuse of the public's trust, and (4) absence of reasonable excuse; the mental element incorporates R v G subjective recklessness; the offence should not routinely be added as an alternative to manslaughter by gross negligence.
legal_issues: What are the ingredients of misconduct in public office
Whether bad faith must be proved and what it means
Whether Cunningham, Sheppard or R v G recklessness applies
Relationship between the tort and crime of misfeasance in public office

notes: Apple Corps v Apple Computer jurisdiction dispute; lengthy but clear findings on place of contracting and Rome Convention.

enrichment.short_title: Apple Corps jurisdiction dispute over 1991 trademark agreement

statutes_considered.title: Rome Convention on the Law Applicable to Contractual Obligations

key_facts: Apple Corps sued Apple Computer alleging breach of a 1991 Trade Mark Agreement regulating use of apple marks in music and computer fields.
Corps claimed Computer's iTunes Music Store breached the agreement by using Apple marks in connection with music delivery.
Service out of the jurisdiction was ordered; Computer disputed jurisdiction on place of contract, governing law and forum conveniens.
The agreement contained no governing law or jurisdiction clause and was completed by transatlantic telephone on 9 October 1991.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application disputing jurisdiction where permission to serve Apple Computer Inc outside the jurisdiction had been granted.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; England was the proper forum; Corps established good arguable case that the contract was made in England (and possibly simultaneously in California), and that English law governed under the Rome Convention.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties deliberately avoided choosing governing law or place of contracting, a contract may be made in two jurisdictions simultaneously for CPR 6.20 purposes; where characteristic performance cannot be determined in a mutual negative covenant trademark agreement, Article 4(1) closest-connection test applies and England was more closely connected given the settlement of prior English litigation; governing law and forum are distinct but English law and England as forum were both established.
legal_issues: Where the 1991 Trade Mark Agreement was made for service out purposes
What law governed the agreement under the Rome Convention
Whether England was the proper forum for the breach claim
Whether a contract can be made in two places at once

notes: Donachie Page v Smith primary victim appeal; judge's foreseeability error and causation findings are clearly reversed.

enrichment.short_title: Police officer's stroke after defective tagging device: Page v Smith applied
key_facts: PC Donachie repeatedly went under a suspect's car to attach a faulty police tracking device during an urgent night operation.
About 30% of new device batteries failed and the force had no testing system despite known reliability problems.
He suffered extreme fear of assault if discovered and subsequently had a stroke linked to stress aggravating pre-existing hypertension unknown to the force.
The trial judge found breach and causation but dismissed for lack of reasonable foreseeability treating him as a secondary victim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of negligence and breach of statutory duty claims; cross-appeal on causation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment for the claimant; case remitted on quantum; the judge erred in applying Sutherland v Hatton rather than Page v Smith as a primary victim with foreseeable physical injury risk.
enrichment.ratio: A police officer exposed to a reasonably foreseeable risk of physical injury from repeated covert visits under a target vehicle is a primary victim; under Page v Smith it is immaterial that the injury was psychiatric injury causing stroke rather than assault; the employer must take the employee as found regarding pre-existing hypertension; defective equipment materially contributing to extreme stress can satisfy causation.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant was a primary or secondary victim for psychiatric injury purposes
Whether pre-existing hypertension affected reasonable foreseeability
Whether faulty batteries materially caused the stroke
Application of Page v Smith and Sutherland v Hatton to police operations

notes: Georgiou planning JR on Truro House; multiple grounds upheld including apparent bias from CAG dual membership.

enrichment.short_title: Truro House planning consent quashed for bias and inadequate reporting
key_facts: Enfield Council granted listed building consent and planning permission for Truro House offices and a 60-bed mental health nursing home in its curtilage.
Four planning committee members also sat on the Conservation Advisory Group, which had expressed support for the scheme.
Officers initially recommended refusal but revised their report after Cygnet submitted amended proposals; the committee approved by 8 votes to 7.
The claimant, a local business association chairman, challenged bias, highways concerns, healthcare need information and consultation reporting.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of planning committee decisions granting listed building consent and planning permission subject to a section 106 agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Decisions and subsequent formal consents quashed on all four grounds; leave to appeal refused on the merits grounds though the bias issue was acknowledged as finely balanced.
enrichment.ratio: Dual membership of the Conservation Advisory Group and planning committee can create an appearance of bias under Porter v Magill where CAG support is carried into planning decisions without qualification; officers must ensure members receive adequate information on highways objections, maintained NHS and social services objections on need, and consultation responses under section 54A.
legal_issues: Whether CAG/planning committee overlap created apparent bias
Whether Mr Juer's highways concerns should have been reported to members
Whether members were misled about healthcare need objections
Whether consultation responses and planning panel notes were adequately summarised
